entities.name: Aave
entities.asset_strategy:
**Asset strategy.** Aave v3 on Ethereum runs the widest curated asset list of the five protocols, 67 reserves in the Core market alone as returned by the [Aave v3 GraphQL API](https://aave.com/docs/aave-v3/getting-started/graphql.md), and it manages that breadth with tiering rather than exclusion: blue chip collateral (WETH, wstETH, WBTC, cbBTC) keeps a full loan to value, while a large second tier of yield bearing and synthetic dollar assets (USDe, sUSDe, rsETH, osETH, DAI, LINK, XAUt) is set to LTV 0 so it can only be used inside E-Mode or as pure supply, with a liquidation threshold still active to protect legacy positions. Almost every non trivial reserve carries an explicit supply cap and borrow cap, and dozens of borrow caps are set to the sentinel value 1, which switches an asset to collateral only in practice. Pricing is standardised on Chainlink feeds wrapped in Aave's own capped adapters (CAPO), described in the [Aave oracle documentation](https://aave.com/docs/ecosystem/oracle.md) as the two oracle types in production. The strategic distinguishing feature is the risk steward and guardian layer: after the April 2026 rsETH bridge exploit the Guardian froze rsETH, wrsETH and even WETH across deployments within hours, per the [Aave rsETH incident report](https://governance.aave.com/t/rseth-incident-report-april-20-2026/24580), which is why several large reserves in the table below sit frozen or at LTV 0 today.

Market: Aave v3 Ethereum Core, Pool `0x87870Bca3F3fD6335C3F4ce8392D69350B4fA4E2`. Parameters read from [the Pool contract](https://etherscan.io/address/0x87870Bca3F3fD6335C3F4ce8392D69350B4fA4E2#readProxyContract); price sources from [AaveOracle](https://etherscan.io/address/0x54586bE62E3c3580375aE3723C145253060Ca0C2#readContract). Ranked by reserve size in USD from the [Aave GraphQL API](https://aave.com/docs/aave-v3/getting-started/graphql.md).

risks.risk: Automatic slashing of staked aTokens under Umbrella
risks.description: Umbrella is the automated Safety Module: users stake aTokens and are slashed automatically when a deficit is recorded, isolated per asset and network pair. Stakers therefore bear first loss on the specific reserve they backstop.
risks.current_mitigation: Isolation per asset and network pair, plus DAO deficit offsets such as the first 100,000 USDT absorbed by the DAO
risks.monitoring_signal: Recorded deficit per Umbrella reserve versus the staked backstop balance for that reserve

risks.risk: Backstop capacity too small for a tail deficit
risks.description: Umbrella was sized against historical deficits of roughly 0.000004 percent of outstanding borrows per month, a scale far below the rsETH shortfall. A single collateral-issuer failure can produce a deficit orders of magnitude larger than the modelled base rate.
risks.current_mitigation: Deficit offsets, staged loss waterfall from stakers to depositors to the DAO treasury
risks.monitoring_signal: Ratio of Umbrella staked value to the largest single-asset exposure in each reserve

risks.risk: Novel V4 Hub and Spoke architecture
risks.description: Aave V4 activated on Ethereum mainnet with Core, Prime and Plus hubs and asset-specific spokes, a materially different design from V3. New code paths mean new unknown failure modes despite extensive review.

risks.monitoring_signal: Unexpected reverts or accounting drift in hub and spoke reconciliation, and any deviation between hub-level and spoke-level accounting

risks.risk: Cross-hub credit line contagion
risks.description: V4 supports cross-hub credit lines, letting liquidity and therefore losses propagate between Core, Prime and Plus. A deficit that starts in one spoke can be transmitted to hubs that never listed the impaired asset.
risks.current_mitigation: Add caps and draw caps per spoke, plus Protocol Security Council emergency powers during the hardening period
risks.monitoring_signal: Drawn amount on each cross-hub credit line versus its draw cap, and change in cross-hub exposure per epoch

entities.risk_posture: Aave's risk profile has shifted decisively from smart contract risk toward collateral issuer and counterparty risk. The core lending logic has held up, but the protocol's willingness to list high-LTV liquid restaking collateral means that a failure anywhere in a partner's minting or bridging stack becomes an Aave solvency event, which is exactly what happened with Kelp and LayerZero in April 2026 ([LlamaRisk](https://governance.aave.com/t/rseth-incident-2026-04-18/24481)). The protocol's crisis machinery works: Guardian freezes were executed within hours and roughly 54 percent of the shortfall was recovered ([TokenLogic](https://governance.aave.com/t/arfc-rseth-incident-funding-update/24740)). What is weak is loss absorption. Umbrella was calibrated against historical deficits measured in millionths of a percent of borrows ([Aave docs](https://aave.com/help/umbrella/umbrella)), the treasury is over half AAVE and buybacks are paused ([Aave governance](https://governance.aave.com/t/arfc-pause-aave-buybacks/24686)), and the residual gap is being closed by a voluntary coalition rather than by protocol capital. Layered on top is a freshly activated V4 hub and spoke architecture with cross-hub credit lines and model-based oracle adapters ([Aave governance](https://governance.aave.com/t/arfc-aave-v4-activation-on-ethereum-mainnet/24293)), which raises technological risk during the hardening period. Net posture: high severity, issuer-driven, with mitigation depending on discretionary emergency powers and external goodwill.

entities.name: Compound
entities.asset_strategy:
**Asset strategy.** Compound III (Comet) does not run a shared pool. Each market has one borrowable base asset and a short list of collateral that can only be used to borrow that base, which structurally isolates every asset pair, as set out in the [Compound III documentation](https://docs.compound.finance/). On Ethereum there are six live markets: USDC, USDT, WETH, WBTC, wstETH and USDS. Collateral is capped in native units, and Compound uses a two factor system, a `borrowCollateralFactor` for opening capacity and a higher `liquidateCollateralFactor` for solvency, with a separate `liquidationFactor` penalty; the liquidator's discount is `StoreFrontPriceFactor * (1e18 - liquidationFactor)` per [the liquidation docs](https://docs.compound.finance/liquidation/). The distinguishing feature is how aggressively Compound deprecates: assets it wants to remove are left listed with a supply cap of 0 and a liquidate factor of 0.0001, which is exactly how deUSD and sdeUSD read today after the Elixir collapse. In the tables the "Liq. bonus" column is the implied penalty, 1 minus liquidationFactor.

Parameters read from each Comet proxy. Bases: USDC `0xc3d688B66703497DAA19211EEdff47f25384cdc3`, USDT `0x3Afdc9BCA9213A35503b077a6072F3D0d5AB0840`, WETH `0xA17581A9E3356d9A858b789D68B4d866e593aE94`, WBTC `0xe85Dc543813B8c2CFEaAc371517b925a166a9293`, wstETH `0x3D0bb1ccaB520A66e607822fC55BC921738fAFE3`, USDS `0x5D409e56D886231aDAf00c8775665AD0f9897b56`.

risks.risk: Governance proposal code defects reaching production
risks.description: Proposal 62 shipped a comparison operator bug, greater-than instead of greater-than-or-equal, in two locations of the reward distribution logic. Roughly 280,000 COMP worth about 82.88 million USD became claimable in error.

risks.risk: Oracle upgrade breaking a live market
risks.description: Proposal 117 upgraded the price oracle to a version that assumed every cToken exposes an underlying() function, which cETH does not, so getUnderlyingPrice reverted. The cETH market was frozen for supply, borrow, withdraw and liquidation for eight days.
risks.current_mitigation: Proposal 119 restored a working feed, and OpenZeppelin published a public post-mortem

risks.risk: Oracle price diverging from tradeable market price on yield-bearing stables

risks.monitoring_signal: Oracle price minus secondary market price for every yield-bearing collateral, alerting above a fixed basis point gap

incidents.what_happened: The DAI price rose to 1.30 USD on Coinbase Pro and the oracle passed the price through, triggering mass liquidations in the DAI market.
incidents.outcome: A compensation proposal based on the 8 percent liquidation penalty was drafted, but the initial executive vote failed with 680,000 COMP against and 212,000 COMP for.

incidents.what_happened: Proposal 62, "Dynamic COMP reward distribution", contained a greater-than instead of greater-than-or-equal comparison in two locations, placing roughly 280,000 COMP at risk of erroneous claim.
incidents.outcome: No supplied or borrowed user funds were at risk; the exposure was limited to the COMP reward pool.

incidents.what_happened: Proposal 117 upgraded the oracle to a version assuming every cToken implements underlying(); cETH does not, so getUnderlyingPrice reverted and the cETH market froze for supply, borrow, withdraw and liquidation.
incidents.outcome: Proposal 119 executed at 01:18 UTC on 7 September 2022 and restored the feed; OpenZeppelin published a post-mortem and no direct loss occurred.

incidents.what_happened: Following the 117 million USD Mango Markets exploit, Compound governance paused YFI, ZRX, BAT and MKR as collateral over price manipulation risk.
incidents.outcome: The proposal passed with 99 percent support and the four assets were removed from active collateral use.

incidents.what_happened: Proposal 289, led by the whale Humpy and The Golden Boys, passed and would have automatically deployed 24 million USD of treasury funds into a goldCOMP product on execution.
incidents.outcome: A truce was reached, the proposal was withdrawn and the deployment was cancelled; a replacement staking product endorsed by OpenZeppelin and Gauntlet was pursued instead.

incidents.what_happened: A market-wide crash with BTC down over 12 percent and ETH down over 20 percent, from 4,354 to 3,435 USD, produced 438 liquidations across Compound comets.
incidents.outcome: V3 Ethereum USDC absorbed the largest share at 15.4 million USD or 38 percent; bad debt stayed under 1,600 USD, mostly on Unichain, and about 1.49 million USD was added to reserves.

incidents.what_happened: An Elixir liquidity crunch hit deUSD and sdeUSD, which were listed as collateral on the Ethereum USDC, USDS and USDT comets; the sdeUSD oracle showed 1.06 while the market price was 0.86.
incidents.outcome: Gauntlet triggered an emergency withdraw-pause, keeping supply and repay open while blocking borrow and withdraw, and characterised the oracle gap as a vulnerability.

entities.risk_posture: Compound's history is dominated by oracle and governance failures rather than direct contract exploits, and the pattern is remarkably consistent across six years. The November 2020 DAI liquidations, the 2022 cETH feed freeze and the November 2025 Elixir sdeUSD gap are all the same failure class: the protocol's internal price diverged from the tradeable price and the system acted on the wrong number ([Compound forum](https://www.comp.xyz/t/proposal-distribute-dai-to-users-affected-by-dai-liquidations/2110), [OpenZeppelin post-mortem](https://www.comp.xyz/t/ceth-price-feed-incident-post-mortem/3578), [Gauntlet](https://www.comp.xyz/t/gauntlet-pausing-ethereum-usdc-usds-and-usdt-comets/7326)). On the governance side, both the 2021 reward distribution bug and the 2024 Humpy treasury proposal show that executable code can reach production with insufficient review or insufficient community control ([CryptoSlate](https://cryptoslate.com/how-the-tiniest-of-errors-resulted-in-an-80-million-loss-for-compound-finance/), [The Block](https://www.theblock.co/post/308215/compound-reaches-truce-with-crypto-whale-humpy-after-controversial-vote-to-move-24-million-in-tokens)). The offsetting strength is that core solvency has been robust: the October 2025 crash produced 438 liquidations and under 1,600 USD of bad debt ([Gauntlet](https://www.comp.xyz/t/gauntlet-compound-market-downturn-analysis-10-10-2025/7297)). The team itself has named the structural weakness, that v3 forces all-or-nothing pauses, and the v4 roadmap is an explicit response with isolated margin assets, asset-level pauses and a new oracle design ([Compound v4 roadmap](https://www.comp.xyz/t/recreating-compound-v4-platform-roadmap/7529)). Net posture: medium severity, oracle and governance driven, with credible remediation in flight but not yet shipped.

entities.name: Morpho
entities.asset_strategy: **Asset strategy.** Morpho has no protocol level asset list at all. Anyone can deploy an immutable market defined by a collateral token, a loan token, an LLTV and an oracle, so "supported assets" means whichever markets curators and vaults have actually funded. There are no supply or borrow caps at the market level; exposure limits live in the ERC-4626 vaults that allocate into markets. Liquidation incentive is derived from LLTV rather than set per asset, and [the Morpho liquidation documentation](https://docs.morpho.org/build/borrow/concepts/liquidation/) states that at an LLTV of 86 percent the liquidation incentive factor is approximately 1.05, a 5 percent bonus, with the protocol taking no fee; Morpho does not publish the general formula on that page, so bonuses at other LLTVs are marked n.a. below. The practical consequence is that Morpho's Ethereum book is dominated by a handful of LLTV tiers (86, 91.5, 94.5, 96.5 percent) and by long tail collateral that no shared pool would list: tokenised credit tranches, Pendle principal tokens, RWA style yield tokens and curator specific dollars. risks.risk: Unlicensed curators making unilateral risk decisions
risks.description: Curator TVL grew from 300 million USD to 7 billion USD, a 2,200 percent increase, with the top five curators holding roughly 43 percent share and no major curator licensed. Depositors delegate credit decisions to entities with no regulatory obligation and no capital at risk.
risks.current_mitigation: Role separation into Owner, Curator, Allocator and Sentinel, timelocks, abdication, gates, adapter registry and fee caps of 50 percent performance and 5 percent management
risks.monitoring_signal: Curator AUM concentration, and the delay between a new market listing and its first published risk rationale
risks.linked_counterparties: Gauntlet, Steakhouse, MEV Capital, Re7, Sentora, 9summits
risks.source: [Chorus One on DeFi curators in 2025](https://chorus.one/reports-research/defi-curators-in-2025-navigating-chaos-building-resilience), [Morpho risk docs](https://docs.morpho.org/learn/resources/risks/)

risks.risk: Hardcoded oracle prices blocking liquidation
risks.description: Stream Finance vault oracles hardcoded xUSD near one dollar, so when the token collapsed liquidations could not trigger and utilisation hit 100 percent. Bad debt ran into the hundreds of millions across at least fifteen Morpho vaults plus Euler.
risks.current_mitigation: Post-incident scrutiny of hardcoded and rate-based oracles, and market close-only settings
risks.monitoring_signal: Any market where the oracle is a fixed constant or an internal exchange rate rather than a market-derived price
risks.linked_counterparties: Stream Finance, MEV Capital, Re7, Euler

risks.risk: Donation-based inflation attack with a faulty oracle
risks.description: Morpho's own documentation warns that on Vaults V1 an attacker can donate into a market with a mispriced oracle and inflict losses on the vault, and that supply caps do not protect against this. A market sitting in the withdrawal queue with a cap of zero is still vulnerable and the loss is unbounded by the cap.
risks.current_mitigation: Documented warning, adapter registry, and guidance to remove markets entirely rather than only zeroing caps
risks.monitoring_signal: Any vault holding a market with a non-market oracle, and unexpected share balance increases in a vault it did not initiate

risks.risk: LP-token oracle manipulation via flash loan
risks.description: The Aerodrome sAMM-cUSDO/USDC LP oracle read raw pool reserves combined with a Chainlink USDC feed, a cUSDO ERC-4626 rate and a hardcoded one dollar USDO price. An attacker flash-loaned 6,666,666.67 USDC, inflated the LP value, borrowed 363,935 USDC and self-liquidated.
risks.current_mitigation: Market set to close-only with allocations zeroed, and the curator fully compensated the 49,303.14 USDC of bad debt
risks.monitoring_signal: Any oracle that reads spot AMM reserves, and any collateral whose price includes a hardcoded stablecoin leg

risks.risk: Last-depositor bank run in Vaults V1.1
risks.description: Morpho documents that in Vault V1.1 the last depositor to exit bears the bad debt left in the vault. This creates a rational incentive to withdraw first at the earliest sign of trouble.
risks.current_mitigation: Documented explicitly, plus Sentinel role and timelocks to slow adverse changes
risks.monitoring_signal: Withdrawal velocity relative to vault liquidity, and any vault where realised bad debt is not yet socialised

risks.risk: Adapter removal frontrunning
risks.description: Removing an adapter without first setting its caps to zero can be frontrun, letting an attacker act between the two operations. This is an operational sequencing hazard rather than a code defect.
risks.current_mitigation: Documented requirement to zero caps before calling removeAdapter
risks.monitoring_signal: Any removeAdapter transaction not preceded by a cap-zeroing transaction in the same block sequence

risks.risk: Reverting oracle putting a market into a degraded state
risks.description: If an oracle reverts, borrow and liquidate calls revert with it, leaving a market that cannot be de-risked. Positions become frozen at whatever health factor they held at the moment of failure.
risks.current_mitigation: Documented degraded-state behaviour so curators can plan a fallback
risks.monitoring_signal: Oracle call revert rate per market, and time since the last successful price update

risks.risk: Curator and venue concentration
risks.description: The top three curators, Steakhouse, Sentora and Gauntlet, together managed about 5.14 billion USD, and Morpho was the largest single venue at 2.91 billion USD. A single curator's error propagates across a large share of the deposit base.
risks.current_mitigation: Vault-level isolation and per-vault caps, plus public curator dashboards
risks.monitoring_signal: Share of protocol TVL controlled by the top three curators, and overlap of the same collateral across their vaults
risks.linked_counterparties: Steakhouse, Sentora, Gauntlet, MEV Capital, Re7

risks.risk: Withdrawal queuing and rate spikes during stress
risks.description: During the Stream Finance fallout withdrawals were queued and rates spiked as high as 190 percent, with 80 percent of withdrawals completing within three days. Even Steakhouse and Gauntlet USDC vaults that had no xUSD exposure became briefly illiquid.
risks.current_mitigation: Interest rate curves that price scarcity, and withdrawal queues that avoid a disorderly first-mover race
risks.monitoring_signal: Vault utilisation at or near 100 percent, and the length of the withdrawal queue in hours

risks.risk: Curator discretion used against borrowers
risks.description: In the PT-USD0++ / USDC vault, users complained that curators cut the supply allocation to 20 million USD and drove rates to three figures for up to 30 hours, which they characterised as punitive. The curator justified it by an imbalanced Pendle SY/PT pool that limited liquidation capacity.
risks.current_mitigation: Public forum disclosure of curator rationale, and Morpho's documented role and timelock framework
risks.monitoring_signal: Sudden allocation cuts and borrow rate jumps in a vault with no corresponding collateral price move

risks.risk: Public Allocator enabling cross-vault contagion
risks.description: After the Resolv exploit, 6.2 million USD of bad debt reached Morpho vaults via the Public Allocator, with Gauntlet accounting for 96 percent of the total losses. Morpho's supply() accepts an onBehalf parameter, so anyone can credit market shares to a vault without its authorisation.
risks.current_mitigation: Curators setting supply caps to zero on affected markets, and a compensation plan announced
risks.monitoring_signal: Inbound supply() calls naming a vault as onBehalf that the vault did not initiate

risks.risk: Over-reliance on third-party risk endorsements
risks.description: Steakhouse Financial published a report five days before the Resolv hack calling the protocol institutionally rigorous and crisis-ready, and other curators used it to justify exposure. Steakhouse itself had no direct USR exposure while the curators relying on its work took the losses.
risks.current_mitigation: Public post-incident scrutiny and calls for higher due diligence, real-time monitoring and built-in circuit breakers
risks.monitoring_signal: Whether a curator's allocation rationale rests on its own analysis or on another party's published report

risks.risk: Immutable core with no parameter correction path
risks.description: Morpho's core is immutable and the LLTV of a market cannot be changed once created. A market created with an unsafe LLTV or oracle can only be abandoned, never fixed.
risks.current_mitigation: Immutability audited by Certora formal verification, with a Cantina bug bounty of 2,500,000 USD
risks.monitoring_signal: Number of live markets flagged as unsafe that remain listed because they cannot be reparameterised

risks.risk: Front-end and SDK misconfiguration routing approvals
risks.description: On 10 April 2025 a front-end and SDK misconfiguration sent token approvals to the Bundler3 contract instead of the intended adapters. One user's bundled transaction was intercepted, though by a whitehat MEV bot rather than an attacker.
risks.current_mitigation: Rollback within four minutes, contracts themselves unaffected, public incident write-up
risks.monitoring_signal: Approval targets in front-end transactions diverging from the canonical adapter address list

risks.risk: Vault shares used as collateral
risks.description: Morpho documentation states that Vault V1.0 is not recommended for use as collateral. Recursive use of vault shares stacks oracle, bad debt and liquidity risk from the underlying markets into a single collateral token.
risks.current_mitigation: Explicit documentation warning, and the V1.1 revision
risks.monitoring_signal: Any market listing a V1.0 vault share as collateral, and the underlying market composition of that vault

risks.risk: Structural leverage inside collateral issuers
risks.description: Stream Finance reached a peak TVL of 520 million USD on 160 million USD of deposits, implying 3.25 times structural leverage, before disclosing a 93 million USD external manager loss on 4 November 2025. Morpho markets accepted the resulting token as collateral without visibility into that leverage.
risks.current_mitigation: Post-incident emphasis on issuer transparency, and market close-only settings after the fact
risks.monitoring_signal: Issuer TVL divided by verifiable external deposits, and any refusal or delay in publishing reserve attestations

entities.risk_posture: Morpho has almost no protocol-level risk and almost all of its risk in the layer above it. The immutable core is formally verified by Certora with a 2.5 million USD Cantina bounty ([Morpho docs](https://docs.morpho.org/learn/resources/risks/)), and in three documented loss events the core behaved exactly as specified. The damage came from curators: who they listed, what oracles they accepted and how fast they reacted. Every major loss traces to a collateral issuer failing while an oracle told the market nothing was wrong, in the Aerodrome LP case ([ClearstarLabs](https://forum.morpho.org/t/post-mortem-aerodrome-cusdo-usdc-amm-lp-oracle-manipulation-on-morpho-lending-market/1794)), in Stream's hardcoded xUSD price ([TokenIntel](https://tokenintel.org/reports/stream-finance-post-mortem-2026-05-21.html)) and in Resolv's hardcoded USR oracle exploited through the Public Allocator ([Oak Research](https://oakresearch.io/en/analyses/investigations/the-resolv-usr-hack-curators-face-their-responsibilities)). Morpho's own documentation is unusually candid about the residual hazards, including donation attacks that supply caps do not stop and the last-depositor bank run in Vaults V1.1 ([Morpho security considerations](https://docs.morpho.org/curate/concepts/security-considerations/)). The structural problem is that curator TVL grew 2,200 percent to 7 billion USD with no licensing and heavy concentration in five firms ([Chorus One](https://chorus.one/reports-research/defi-curators-in-2025-navigating-chaos-building-resilience)). Net posture: low technological risk in the base layer, critical and recurring counterparty and governance risk in the curated layer, with loss magnitude driven almost entirely by curator judgement.

entities.asset_strategy:
**Asset strategy.** Radiant is in wind down and should not be read as a live venue. The DAO began winding down on 1 June 2026, having never recovered from the October 2024 DPRK linked exploit that drained about $50M; TVL across all four chains was about $2.21M on 1 June 2026, split roughly Arbitrum $939k, Ethereum $468k, Base $458k and BNB Chain $343k, and RDNT had already been delisted by OKX, Crypto.com and finally Binance, per [The Defiant](https://thedefiant.io/news/defi/radiant-capital-winds-down-2m-husk-dprk-50m-heist). The [protocol sunset technical reference](https://docs.radiant.capital/radiant/protocol-sunset/technical-reference) states that the lending pool borrow parameter has been set to 1, which effectively disables borrowing, that RDNT emissions have ended, and that deposits, withdrawals, repayments and liquidations still function, with Chainlink adapters continuing to read live feeds. That is exactly what the contracts show: on both the Arbitrum and Ethereum pools every borrowable reserve reads a borrow cap of 1. Historical loan to value and liquidation threshold values are still stored on chain, and they are reported below as stored values, not as an invitation to use the protocol. Radiant's asset strategy when live was Arbitrum first, with GMX ecosystem collateral (GM and GLV tokens) that no other protocol in this set lists, plus a RIZ isolated market layer.

Arbitrum core pool `0xE23B4AE3624fB6f7cDEF29bC8EAD912f1Ede6886`, Ethereum core pool `0xA950974f64aA33f27F6C5e017eEE93BF7588ED07`, both listed in the [Radiant contracts documentation](https://docs.radiant.capital/radiant/contracts-and-security/arbitrum-contracts) and [Ethereum contracts documentation](https://docs.radiant.capital/radiant/contracts-and-security/ethereum-contracts). All liquidation bonuses read 15 percent.

Other Ethereum reserves read the same way and are omitted for space: USDT 75/78, WBTC 73/78, sDAI 77/80, rETH 75/80, weETH 72.5/75, LINK 65/70, USDS 77/80, tBTC 70/75, UNI 65/70, cbBTC 73/78, cbETH 75/80, PYUSD 72/75, LBTC 73/78, PAXG 60/68 and AAVE 65/70, all with a 15 percent liquidation bonus, all read from [the Ethereum pool](https://etherscan.io/address/0xA950974f64aA33f27F6C5e017eEE93BF7588ED07#readProxyContract).

entities.risk_posture: Radiant is no longer a going concern and its risk profile should be read as exit risk, not lending risk. Two exploits inside ten months, a roughly 720 ETH shortfall from a flash loan against an empty new market in January 2024 ([Radiant post-mortem](https://medium.com/@RadiantCapital/post-mortem-report-radiant-capital-aea46cb985ae)) and about 50 million USD from a device-malware multisig compromise in October 2024 ([Radiant post-mortem](https://medium.com/@RadiantCapital/radiant-post-mortem-fecd6cd38081)), destroyed the protocol's capital base and its trust. Neither loss was recovered, and after eighteen months with no external investment and no grants the DAO began an orderly wind-down on 1 June 2026 ([WuBlockchain](https://www.wublockchain.xyz/news/radiant-capital-wind-down-after-50m-exploit-failure-19380)). The dominant risks now are operational rather than financial: borrowing is disabled with caps at 1, RDNT emissions have stopped, support is best-effort, the front-end only survives through end of year, and the DAO explicitly warns that no further upgrades, patches or interventions should be assumed ([Sunsetting Radiant Capital DAO](https://medium.com/@RadiantCapital/sunsetting-radiant-capital-dao-entering-recovery-phase-and-lessons-for-the-future-of-defi-c47837ffa499)). Some RIZ vault losses were declared permanently irrecoverable ([RIZ post-mortem](https://community.radiant.capital/t/post-mortem-october-16-2024-exploit-impact-on-riz-vaults/2220)). Net posture: critical, terminal, and the only rational user action is capital withdrawal, which is exactly what the DAO itself advises.

entities.name: Spark Protocol
entities.asset_strategy:
**Asset strategy.** Spark is the Sky (formerly MakerDAO) lending arm and its coverage is two different things at once. SparkLend is a deliberately short Aave v3 style collateral list: 18 reserves on Ethereum, of which only WETH, wstETH, WBTC, cbBTC, LBTC and weETH carry a non zero loan to value, while the dollar assets (USDC, USDT, USDS, PYUSD) are configured as pure borrow assets with LTV and liquidation threshold at zero and effectively unlimited caps. [The SparkLend documentation](https://docs.spark.fi/products/sparklend) is explicit that the list is short by design, that ETH e-mode collateral is limited to wstETH and rETH, and that BTC e-mode was removed entirely. The second and larger half of Spark's asset coverage is allocation driven rather than collateral driven: the [Spark Liquidity Layer](https://docs.spark.fi/products/spark-liquidity-layer) moves USDS, USDC and USDT into Sky's PSM, Aave v3 and SparkLend, Spark curated Morpho vaults, Curve and Uniswap stablecoin pools, Ethena USDe and sUSDe, EtherFi weETH, Lido wstETH, Maple redemptions, Superstate USTB and OTC desks across Ethereum, Base, Arbitrum, Optimism, Unichain, Avalanche and Robinhood Chain, all under keccak256 keyed rate limits with a max amount and a refill slope, and any unapproved venue reverts. Spark Savings adds ERC-4626 vaults (spUSDC, spUSDT, spPYUSD, spETH, spUSDG, plus Sky's sUSDS and stUSDS) whose exposure is again allocation rather than collateral, per [the Spark Savings documentation](https://docs.spark.fi/products/spark-savings). So a reader comparing Spark to Aave on collateral lists alone will badly understate its asset footprint.

SparkLend Ethereum, Pool `0xC13e21B648A5Ee794902342038FF3aDAB66BE987` and AaveOracle `0x8105f69D9C41644c6A0803fDA7D03Aa70996cFD9`, both from the [Spark address registry](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/sparkdotfi/spark-address-registry/master/src/SparkLend.sol). All 18 reserves are shown.

Market size context, for scale rather than parameters: the Spark app reported total market size $5.554B, TVL $3.722B and total borrows $1.832B on the Ethereum market, with wstETH at 1.025M supplied and ETH at 484.4K supplied ([Spark markets app](https://app.spark.fi/markets)).

entities.risk_posture: Spark's posture is deliberately conservative on the lending side and aggressive on the balance sheet side, and the two must be assessed separately. SparkLend itself is a hardened Aave v3 fork with a three-oracle median across RedStone, Chainlink and Chronicle, a killswitch peg-ratio oracle, rate-limited caps and a tight collateral set that excludes BTC e-mode entirely ([SparkLend docs](https://docs.spark.fi/products/sparklend)). That conservatism paid off when the January 2026 deprecation spell froze rsETH three months before the Kelp exploit, leaving Spark with no direct exposure and attracting 1.4 billion USD of fleeing Aave deposits ([Sky executive vote](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/sky-ecosystem/executive-votes/main/2026/executive-vote-2026-01-29-msc-pattern-and-skybase-onboarding.md), [Streetbrief](https://www.streetbrief.co/article/spark-protocol-captures-1-4b-inflow-kelp-dao-exploit-triggers-aave-liquidity-crisis-2604/)). The real risk sits in the Spark Liquidity Layer, which allocates up to 1.1 billion USD directly to Ethena's USDe and sUSDe plus 200 million DAI to Pendle PT markets ([Spark mirror post](https://mirror.xyz/0xF99d0E4E3435cc9C9868D1C6274DfaB3e2721341/LjBAybIk6-waSxwOBWp5mg_37jNvrWF_UdzqqXoEl6U)) and routes capital across CCTP, LayerZero, Maple and Superstate via a relayer whose own threat model assumes it can be fully compromised ([SLL docs](https://docs.spark.fi/products/spark-liquidity-layer)). Loss absorption is unusually deep, six layers ending in SKY token issuance and equal socialisation across USDS holders ([Spark Savings docs](https://docs.spark.fi/products/spark-savings)), but that final layer means Spark depositors are ultimately Sky creditors. Net posture: low protocol risk, concentrated issuer and operational risk on the treasury side, with the strongest incident record of the five.

entities.name: Extra Finance
entities.asset_strategy: Extra Finance runs two distinct products with two completely different asset surfaces. The older one is **leveraged yield farming (LYF)**, where the "supported asset" is not a single token but an **AMM LP pool** on Velodrome (Optimism) or Aerodrome (Base): the user deposits one or both pool tokens, borrows the pool tokens from Extra's lending reserves, and the protocol mints an LP position that is auto-compounded. Risk is expressed per farming vault as a **Liquidation Threshold stated as a maximum Debt Ratio** plus a **maximum leverage multiple**, not as a per-token LTV, and every farming vault has its own numeric Vault ID ([Extra Finance Pool Info](https://docs.extrafi.io/extra_finance/leverage-farming/pool-info)). The second product is **XLend**, an Aave v3 fork on Base and Optimism with conventional per-reserve LTV, liquidation threshold, liquidation bonus, supply cap, borrow cap, E-Mode and isolation-mode debt ceilings ([XLend E-Mode docs](https://docs.extrafi.io/extrafi-xlend/borrow-lend/e-mode), [XLend Isolation Mode docs](https://docs.extrafi.io/extrafi-xlend/borrow-lend/isolation-mode)). What distinguishes Extra is the split oracle philosophy between the two: LYF prices positions off the AMM curve itself with a TWAP and a Chainlink deviation guard, while XLend uses Chainlink as primary ([Extra Finance Price Feed](https://docs.extrafi.io/extra_finance/leverage-farming/price-feed), [XLend Price Feed](https://docs.extrafi.io/extrafi-xlend/borrow-lend/price-feed)). The XLend docs "Parameters" page is published but empty, so all XLend numbers below were read directly from the on-chain Aave v3 `Pool.getConfiguration(address)` reserve configuration bitmap on Base pool `0x09b11746dfd1b5a8325e30943f8b3d5000922e03` and Optimism pool `0x345D2827f36621b02B783f7D5004B4a2fec00186` on 2026-07-26, the Optimism pool address being the one published by Extra ([Extra Finance contracts](https://docs.extrafi.io/extra_finance/contracts-and-transparency)). Total protocol TVL is roughly $27M, concentrated on Base ([DefiLlama Extra Finance](https://defillama.com/protocol/extra-finance)).

entities.risk_posture: Extra Finance is a small and shrinking leveraged farming protocol whose risk is concentrated rather than systemic. The design is conservative in places: partial liquidation at 30% of a position, an 8% fee on only the liquidated slice, per-asset caps in XLend, no admin withdrawal function and a self-imposed rule to disable leverage when its own liquidity share of a farmed pool exceeds about 30%. Against that, the protocol depends on a team-operated liquidation bot for the farming product, on a 30-minute on-chain TWAP that is manipulable in shallow markets, and on two OP Stack chains for essentially all of its book. The February 2025 EXA bad debt event shows the failure mode is real, and the collapse in TVL from roughly $117m in August 2024 to about $24m today means both revenue and the liquidity cushion that keeps liquidations orderly are much thinner than when the parameters were designed.

entities.name: Fluid
entities.asset_strategy:
Fluid's core innovation is that a **vault is the unit of listing, not a token**, and both sides of a vault can be a **DEX position rather than a plain ERC-20**. In classic Fluid vaults the collateral token and the debt token are ordinary assets, but in **smart collateral** vaults the deposit is an LP share of a Fluid DEX pool, and in **smart debt** vaults the borrowing itself is a DEX position so the borrower earns trading fees on the debt leg while paying borrow interest. Vault 44 on Ethereum, wstETH-ETH collateral against wstETH-ETH debt, is smart collateral plus smart debt at once, and vault 51, WBTC-cbBTC against WBTC-cbBTC, is the BTC analogue. This means "supported asset" for Fluid has to be read as an ordered pair plus a mode, and the same underlying token can appear with materially different collateral factors depending on the pairing. Fluid also runs a **dual-oracle design** where the price used to permit an operation can differ from the price used to permit a liquidation, and vault upgrades are shipped by deploying new vault versions and winding down the old ones over months rather than by mutating parameters in place ([Fluid governance, Deploy Fluid upgrades to Vault protocol](https://gov.fluid.io/t/deploy-fluid-upgrades-to-vault-protocol/764), [MixBytes analysis of the Fluid vault](https://mixbytes.io/blog/modern-defi-lending-protocols-how-its-made-fluid-vault)). Every parameter row below was read live on 2026-07-26 from the Fluid public vault API for each chain, for example [api.fluid.instadapp.io/v2/1/vaults](https://api.fluid.instadapp.io/v2/1/vaults). Protocol TVL is roughly $797M ([DefiLlama Fluid](https://defillama.com/protocol/fluid)).

Column mapping for Fluid: "Max LTV %" is the vault `collateralFactor`, "Liq. threshold %" is `liquidationThreshold`, "Liq. bonus %" is `liquidationPenalty`, "Supply cap" is the liquidity layer `baseWithdrawalLimit` in collateral-token units, and "Borrow cap" is `maxBorrowLimit` in debt-token units. Fluid additionally publishes a `liquidationMaxLimit` (LML), the hard ceiling above which a position can be fully liquidated, which is reported in Notes.

entities.risk_posture: Fluid is the most technically sophisticated protocol in this set and also the one with the most recent damage. Its shared Liquidity Layer and tick-based liquidation engine allow 80% to 95% LTVs with penalties as low as 0.1%, which is genuinely best in class, and Yearn's curation team scored it 1.4 out of 5.0, "Minimal Risk". The problem is not the engine, it is what gets plugged into it: Fluid repeatedly ends up holding almost the entire float of a third-party yield-bearing wrapper inside 6x loops, so an issuer failure at Resolv in March 2026 turned into $10m to $21m of Fluid bad debt and a 30% TVL fall in a day. Bad debt was made whole, but by discretionary loans and a team multisig drawing a credit line before the governance vote, which is a governance answer rather than a structural one, and the one-day timelock leaves lenders little room to act on such decisions. Today's book still shows top-five collateral at 69% and several markets above 90% utilization, so the same shape is in place, and the Jupiter Lend and Venus deployments extend that shape to venues Fluid does not run.

entities.name: Gearbox
entities.asset_strategy:
Gearbox is the protocol where "supported asset" is least meaningful as a flat list. Liquidity providers deposit into an **underlying-asset pool**, for example a WETH, wstETH, USDC, USDT, DAI, GHO, crvUSD, WBTC, tBTC or DOLA pool, each pool owned by a named **curator**. A borrower opens a **credit account**, a smart contract wallet that holds borrowed funds plus their own collateral, and each pool is served by one or more **credit managers** that define, per credit manager, the exact list of tokens that may sit in the account and the **liquidation threshold** applied to each. On top of that, a credit account can only interact with the outside world through **adapters**, whitelisted contracts that translate a call into an allowed action against a specific integrated protocol such as Curve, Convex, Pendle, Balancer, Uniswap, Lido, Mellow or a specific ERC-4626 vault. The asset surface is therefore the cross product of collateral tokens with per-manager liquidation thresholds, quota limits set in the PoolQuotaKeeper which act as a per-collateral borrow cap, and the adapter whitelist. Gearbox documents its price layer as "Chainlink Price Feeds, Redstone Price Feeds as well as some composite smart contract oracles", and it documents that "the current version of Gearbox has isolated lending only, in which case the risk is contained within LP pools" ([Gearbox risks and T&C](https://docs.gearbox.finance/developers/risks-and-t-c-2), [Gearbox adapters and integrations](https://docs.gearbox.finance/core/adapters-integrations)). The interest rate model is a two-kink curve with an `isBorrowingMoreU2Forbidden` switch that hard-blocks borrowing past the second kink ([Gearbox interest rate model](https://docs.gearbox.finance/core/interest-rate-model)). All numeric values below were read live on 2026-07-26 from mainnet: 21 pools, 89 credit managers, 227 collateral tokens with liquidation thresholds, and 888 adapters, via the CreditAccountCompressor at 0x4115708Fc8fe6bB392De2e0C21c2C81dA2222394 and the pool and quota-keeper contracts. Gearbox TVL is roughly $18.4M ([DefiLlama Gearbox](https://defillama.com/protocol/gearbox)).

Column mapping for Gearbox: "Max LTV %" is not a Gearbox concept, so it is reported as n.a.; "Liq. threshold %" is the per-credit-manager liquidation threshold, reported as the observed range across credit managers where a token appears in more than one; "Borrow cap" is the PoolQuotaKeeper quota limit for that collateral in the named pool; there is no supply cap primitive.

risks.risk: Curator sets unsafe risk parameters
risks.description: Curators act as Administrator over a Market Configurator and control every risk parameter including liquidation thresholds, quotas and the interest rate model. Wrong liquidation thresholds on allowed assets can make LP pools insolvent, and ChainSecurity notes the Configurator role is fully trusted and can configure most system parameters.
risks.current_mitigation: Administrator changes are subject to a 24-hour minimum timelock; curators must bear first loss via staking under the GIP-264 model; revenue split default 50% curator, 50% DAO.
risks.monitoring_signal: Pending Market Configurator transactions in the 24-hour timelock, and curator stake size versus pool TVL.
risks.linked_counterparties: K3 Capital, Re7 Labs, kpk (formerly karpatkey), Chaos Labs, Maven11, Invariant Group
risks.source: [Gearbox market curators docs](https://docs.gearbox.finance/core/market-curators), [Gearbox risks and T&C](https://docs.gearbox.finance/developers/risks-and-t-c-2), [ChainSecurity V3.1 integrations audit](https://reports.chainsecurity.com/Gearbox/ChainSecurity_Gearbox_GearboxV31Integrations_Audit.pdf)

risks.risk: Emergency Admin bypasses the timelock
risks.description: The Emergency Admin role bypasses the 24-hour timelock and can pause a market, set debt limits to zero and forbid adapters or tokens. It cannot increase risk, but it can freeze a user's ability to manage a leveraged position at the worst moment.
risks.current_mitigation: Role is constrained to risk-reducing actions only; a whitelisted Emergency Liquidator can still liquidate when a market is paused.
risks.monitoring_signal: Emergency Admin transactions and market pause events.
risks.linked_counterparties: Curator Emergency Admin multisigs, Gearbox Veto Admin (3-of-10 or 3-of-12 rapid response multisig)

risks.risk: Oracle failure causing cascading liquidations
risks.description: Gearbox's own risk page states a rogue oracle can cause cascading liquidations and bad debt, and the protocol relies on Chainlink, Redstone and composite smart contract oracles. Composite oracles that derive an exchange rate from another contract inherit that contract's failure modes.
risks.current_mitigation: Dual-oracle design pairs a Main Feed for liquidation with a Reserve Feed acting as a guardrail against incorrect or outdated valuations; Price Feed Store whitelisting is required to create a market.
risks.monitoring_signal: Main Feed versus Reserve Feed deviation per asset, and feed staleness on Redstone push feeds.
risks.linked_assets: ezETH, weETH, rsETH, wstETH, LST and LRT collateral generally
risks.linked_counterparties: Chainlink, Redstone, LST and LRT issuers
risks.source: [Gearbox risks and T&C](https://docs.gearbox.finance/developers/risks-and-t-c-2), [Gearbox oracle design blog](https://blog.gearbox.finance/what-happens-when-oracles-think-twice-permissionless-oracle-design/), [Gearbox create a market](https://docs.gearbox.finance/curators/create-a-market)

risks.risk: Liquidation cascade on LRT depeg
risks.description: Gearbox explicitly cites the April 2024 ezETH cascade as the motivating case for its Loss Policy, when rapid price falls outran liquidators. Leverage of up to 40x on a credit account means small collateral moves are enough to breach a health factor of 1.
risks.current_mitigation: Loss Policy blocks a liquidation that would create bad debt if the position is healthy under an aliased fundamental price; partial liquidation via a Deleverage Bot triggers at a configured minHF such as 1.05 with a reduced premium.
risks.monitoring_signal: Count of accounts with health factor below 1.05, and frequency of Loss Policy blocked liquidations.

risks.risk: Bad debt socialised onto LPs
risks.description: If a Credit Account is liquidated with Total Value below Total Debt, unclaimed protocol fees are burned first and any remaining loss is socialised by reducing the Diesel LP token exchange rate. Lenders, not borrowers, take the residual.
risks.current_mitigation: Fee buffer absorbs first; Loss Policy avoids realising losses at distressed prices; Gearbox reports no bad debt since inception in 2021.
risks.monitoring_signal: Diesel token exchange rate; any non-monotonic move is a realised LP loss.
risks.linked_assets: Diesel LP tokens (dUSDC, dWETH and equivalents)

risks.risk: Loss Policy pausing liquidations during a real repricing
risks.description: The aliased bad debt policy halts liquidation when a position is healthy at fundamental price even though it is underwater at market price. If the market price is correct and the peg never returns, the deferred loss is larger when it is finally realised.
risks.current_mitigation: Aliased pricing is configurable per market, so curators choose the fundamental reference; the fundamental check still permits liquidation when the asset is genuinely insolvent.
risks.monitoring_signal: Duration and notional of positions sitting in Loss Policy blocked state, and market versus aliased price gap.
risks.linked_assets: Stablecoins priced at aliased 1.00, LSTs priced at exchange rate
risks.linked_counterparties: Curators configuring aliased feeds, Price Feed Store

risks.risk: Liquidator dependency and MEV
risks.description: Liquidations depend on third-party liquidators who Gearbox acknowledges may malfunction, and the risks page also flags sandwich and MEV extraction against protocol operations. In small accounts the liquidation premium may not cover gas, which historically left core contributors liquidating at their own expense.
risks.current_mitigation: Token-backed backstops, a Reserve Fund and the recruitment of more professional liquidators; partial liquidation is executed by a specialised Deleverage Bot.
risks.monitoring_signal: Time from health factor below 1 to liquidation, and liquidator address diversity.
risks.linked_counterparties: Independent liquidator bots, Deleverage Bot operator, Ethereum block builders

risks.risk: Adapter and integration surface risk
risks.description: Credit Accounts reach into external protocols through adapters, and Gearbox says credit accounts can connect to assets that are not on DEXes or not even tokenised. Each adapter imports the security assumptions of the target protocol.
risks.current_mitigation: Strict adapter allowlists (kpk's handbook specifies allowlists plus utilisation caps and quota limits); Emergency Admin can forbid an adapter immediately; Bytecode Repository verification ensures only audited bytecode is deployed.
risks.monitoring_signal: New adapter deployments per market, and the number of distinct external protocols reachable from a single credit account.

risks.linked_counterparties: Mellow Finance, Curve, Lido, Pendle, Ethena, Sky, Sigma Prime (V3 integrations auditor)

risks.monitoring_signal: Curator TVL share, and overlap of the same collateral assets across different curators' markets.

risks.description: Gearbox states plainly that an LP cannot withdraw if the pool is fully utilised. Under the Two-Kink interest rate model, curators can also set isBorrowingMoreU2Forbidden to cap borrowing past U2.
risks.current_mitigation: Utilization-dependent interest rate curve with a slope 3 penalty above U2 to force repayment; Tumbler rate keeper adjusts quota rates by epoch.

entities.risk_posture: Gearbox has the strongest loss record of the four, with no bad debt since 2021 including through the April 2024 ezETH cascade where it was the single most affected venue with $33m liquidated and still turned a profit. Its protections are unusually concrete: a dual-oracle Main and Reserve feed, a Loss Policy that halts liquidation when a position is only underwater at a dislocated market price, partial liquidation via a Deleverage Bot at a reduced premium, per-asset quotas that cap how much debt any collateral can secure, formal verification of the math libraries and a $1,000,000 Immunefi bounty. The risk has instead moved to the counterparty layer. Since GIP-264, risk parameters are set by commercial curators such as K3 Capital, Re7 Labs, kpk and Chaos Labs, and Gearbox's own auditor notes the Configurator role is fully trusted; a 24-hour timelock is the only structural brake, and an Emergency Admin can bypass even that. Combine that with credit accounts reaching up to 40x across adapters into Mellow, Pendle, Ethena and Sky, and 27 chains to police, and the plausible failure mode is not a contract bug but one curator parameterising one exotic collateral badly.

entities.name: Stella
entities.asset_strategy: Stella is the outlier in this set because it is largely dormant and its public disclosure effectively stops in 2024. Its model is a **zero-borrowing-interest leveraged strategy protocol on Arbitrum**: lenders deposit a single asset into either a Hyper or a Standard lend pool, and strategy users borrow that liquidity to run a leveraged position on a specific DEX or yield venue, paying the lender a share of profit rather than an interest rate. The unit of listing is therefore a **strategy** (a specific pool on a specific venue with a specific leverage cap) plus a small set of **lendable underlying assets**. Leverage limits are derived from a Collateral Factor and Borrow Factor per strategy rather than published per asset, and Stella states only that "the threshold variable is set to 0.97-0.98.5 based on each strategy" ([Stella leverage docs, page dated 2023-09-29](https://docs.stellaxyz.io/stella-doc/stella-yield/stella-strategy/leverage)). A distinctive and rarely seen mechanic is that **every strategy position expires after 30 days from opening and becomes liquidatable at expiry regardless of health**, in addition to becoming liquidatable when the Debt Ratio exceeds 100% ([Stella liquidation docs, page dated 2024-06-28](https://docs.stellaxyz.io/stella-doc/stella-yield/stella-strategy/liquidation)). Caps exist in two layers, since "each strategy operates with its own specific borrowing cap, in addition to the underlying asset's borrowing cap", but no numeric cap is published ([Stella lend docs](https://docs.stellaxyz.io/stella-doc/stella-yield/stella-lend/why-stella-lend-is-unique)). Staleness is material and should be stated plainly: the supported-strategies page is dated 2023-11-08, the supported-lend-assets page is dated 2023-09-26, the Stella data API at graph.stellaxyz.io returns HTTP error code 522 and is offline, and DefiLlama reports Stella TVL at roughly $443k, Arbitrum only ([Stella supported strategies](https://docs.stellaxyz.io/stella-doc/stella-yield/stella-strategy/supported-strategies), [Stella supported lend assets](https://docs.stellaxyz.io/stella-doc/stella-yield/stella-lend/supported-assets), [DefiLlama Stella](https://defillama.com/protocol/stella)).

entities.risk_posture: Stella is best understood as a small residual protocol carrying a very large unresolved liability from a previous life. The 2021 Alpha Homora V2 exploit left $32.429m owed to Iron Bank, the pledged 50m ALPHA collateral lost more than 90% of its value, repayment ran at about $5,000 a month, and the counterparty responded by freezing roughly $41m of user funds and then walking away from the project entirely in February 2024. That history is not closed and it defines the entity. The current product has some sensible design features, published Collateral Factors of 0.92 to 0.95 per LP, a 2-day lender withdrawal delay against sandwiching, and a documented oracle contingency, but the oracle is off-chain and depends on centralised exchange prices, leverage parameters are set at the research team's discretion rather than on chain, no current audit report was located, positions carry a hard 30-day expiry liquidation, and TVL of $442,829 on Arbitrum alone is far below the liquidity depth any leveraged farming design needs to liquidate cleanly. Successive exchange delistings through 2025 and into 2026 point the same direction. Treat this as a wind-down profile rather than a going-concern leverage venue.

risks.risk: Offchain credit underwriting is unverifiable onchain

risks.risk: Collateral concentration in BTC and XRP
risks.description: Verified onchain collateral was 53.92% BTC at about 667 million USD and 25.38% XRP at about 314 million USD out of about 1.24 billion USD total. A correlated drawdown across these two assets would hit most of the book at once.
risks.current_mitigation: Collateral ratio of about 168.96%, margin call at 85% LTV and liquidation at 90% LTV for BTC, asset level LTV caps
risks.monitoring_signal: Rolling 30 day correlation and drawdown of BTC and XRP against posted collateral value
risks.linked_counterparties: Maple Direct borrowers posting BTC and XRP collateral

risks.current_mitigation: Published impairment policy in Maple documentation, disclosure obligations, third party curation monitoring
risks.monitoring_signal: Any impairment event recorded against the pool, step changes in syrupUSDC exchange rate

incidents.what_happened: A 10 million USDC loan to Babel Finance in the Orthogonal Trading pool on Maple was liquidated. A Notice of Default had been issued on 1 July 2022 for violating a representation in the Master Loan Agreement, and the smart contracts recognised default on 9 July.
incidents.outcome: Pool Cover including an extra 1 million USD deposited on the day was liquidated, but liquidation value is capped at a third of the USDC in the Balancer pool. The remaining 7,852,146 USD was absorbed evenly by lenders in a pool of 244,000,237.40 USD, a 3.2% loss to all lenders.

incidents.what_happened: Auros Global missed the principal payment on a 2,400 wETH loan worth about 3 million USD from an M11 Credit pool, citing a short term liquidity issue caused by the FTX insolvency. Total Auros exposure to the M11 wETH pool was 8,400 wETH, about 10.7 million USD, plus a 7.5 million USDC loan from a second M11 pool.
incidents.outcome: Restructuring rather than write off. M11 Credit recovered an initial 60% in February 2023 and secured full repayment of 7.5 million USDC and 8,400 wETH including interest on 8 November 2023.
incidents.source: [CoinDesk on the Auros missed payment](https://www.coindesk.com/markets/2022/11/30/crypto-trader-auros-global-misses-payment-on-defi-loan-as-ftx-contagion-spreads), [M11 Credit on full repayment](https://medium.com/@M11credit/auros-global-repaid-100-of-funds-to-m11-credit-pools-on-maple-a5509cc1911e)

incidents.what_happened: Orthogonal Trading defaulted on about 36 million USD of loans on Maple, made up of about 31 million USDC across four loans plus roughly 5 million USD in wETH. Maple stated Orthogonal had been operating while effectively insolvent and had misrepresented its financial position, with the losses tied to funds trapped on FTX.
incidents.outcome: Maple severed ties with Orthogonal, M11 Credit issued the default notice, and the loss fell on lenders in the affected pools.

incidents.what_happened: Following the 2022 defaults, Maple wound down its undercollateralised lending model. Deposits that had approached 1 billion USD in May 2022 fell to 21 million USD of TVL in March 2023.
incidents.outcome: All pools launched in 2023 were overcollateralised and only about 10% of outstanding loans remained undercollateralised by September 2023. Maple brought underwriting in house under Maple Direct.

entities.risk_posture: Maple is the most credit heavy protocol in this set, and its risk is fundamentally about who is borrowing rather than about code. It has never suffered a smart contract exploit, but it has suffered real credit losses: lenders took a 3.2% haircut on the Babel liquidation in July 2022 and a roughly 36 million USD default from Orthogonal Trading in December 2022, both traceable to a borrower misstating its position. Maple's answer since then has been to move underwriting in house, require overcollateralisation, and lean on regulated custodians and a Reg D exemption to serve institutional and accredited money, which is a genuine improvement but shifts the exposure rather than removing it. What remains is a concentrated book, more than three quarters of collateral in BTC and XRP, a single externally owned Pool Delegate key, an impairment switch that can cut depositor value without a vote, and secondary liquidity too thin to absorb a large exit. Depositors should treat syrupUSDC as a credit fund with a token wrapper, not as a money market position.

entities.name: Notional Finance
entities.asset_strategy: Notional's original design was a true fixed-term order book: lenders and borrowers trade fCash, a zero-coupon claim on a specific currency at a specific maturity, against Prime Cash on a set tenor ladder of 3 month, 6 month, 1 year, 2 year, 5 year, 10 year and 20 year points, with quarterly rolls and a per-currency `max market index` limiting how far out a currency trades ([Notional fCash maturities docs](https://docs.notional.finance/v3-risk-parameters/fcash-markets/fcash-maturities.md)). Risk is managed through a pairwise collateral framework rather than a single global LTV: each currency has a collateral haircut and a debt buffer, and the effective max LTV falls out of the specific collateral and debt pair ([Notional max LTV parameters sheet](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1Dm6dN5nXqJWhDAV3k313OT3bjqbwQ9qTJ2noq1xJRi0/edit?usp=sharing), linked from the [max LTV table docs page](https://docs.notional.finance/notional-v3/borrower-resources/max-ltv-table.md)). The critical thing to record for July 2026 is that this V3 system is being wound down: after the November 3, 2025 Balancer V2 hack impaired five leveraged vaults, Notional announced a full wind-down of V3 on Mainnet and Arbitrum ([Notional Balancer hack response](https://blog.notional.finance/balancer-hack-response/)). The forward strategy is Notional Exponent, a curated leveraged-vault product that launched January 26, 2026 with only two USDC vaults, mHYPER and mAPOLLO, both built on Midas Protocol tokenized strategies ([Exponent launch details](https://blog.notional.finance/notional-exponent-launch-details/), [Exponent is live](https://blog.notional.finance/notional-exponent-is-live/)).

Protocol reserves of roughly 100 thousand USD on mainnet and 18 thousand USD on Arbitrum were written to zero, plus about 205 thousand USD and 161,450 USD of non ETH reserves converted to ETH. ETH lenders were then haircut 56.019% on mainnet and 19.244% on Arbitrum.

entities.risk_posture: Notional's failure mode was composability, not its own code. Its lending and fCash machinery worked as designed, but its leveraged vaults had deposited user capital into Balancer V2, and when Balancer was exploited in November 2025 the loss travelled straight through: vault holders lost everything, the protocol's reserves proved to be a rounding error against the damage, and mainnet ETH lenders were haircut more than 56%. That is the important lesson, because it shows that in Notional's design the lenders, not an insurance fund, are the ultimate backstop. Rather than recapitalise, the team wound V3 down on both chains and migrated borrowers out to Aave. The successor, Notional Exponent, launched in January 2026 with Sherlock and MixBytes audits, a 250 thousand USD Immunefi bounty and Hypernative monitoring, but it is a new codebase with thin launch liquidity that again depends on external curators and strategy providers. Anyone underwriting Exponent is underwriting the same composability question with better monitoring and no track record yet.

entities.name: Pendle Finance
entities.asset_strategy: Pendle is the volume leader in yield tokenization and its asset strategy is aggressive breadth: any yield-bearing asset that can be wrapped into a Standardized Yield (SY) token can be split into a Principal Token and a Yield Token with a fixed expiry, and Pendle lists across Ethereum, Arbitrum, BNB Chain, Base and Sonic. As of July 26, 2026, chain 1 alone has 58 active markets in the API. The composition of the current top book is telling: it is dominated not by liquid staking tokens but by newer synthetic dollar and RWA-flavoured assets (USDai, USDat, sUSDe, sUSDD, mAPOLLO, mHYPER, ynRWAx, superUSDC), with Lido wstETH the only large legacy LSD market and the only one running out to December 2027. The single largest market by liquidity is PT-USDai on Arbitrum at $50.4M, an order of magnitude above the next tier. What distinguishes Pendle from Spectra is the depth per market and the fact that its PT pricing has become infrastructure for other protocols: the Linear Discount Oracle is explicitly positioned as the recommended feed for money markets and has been adopted by Aave and Morpho curators including Gauntlet and Steakhouse ([Pendle oracle overview](https://docs.pendle.finance/pendle-v2-dev/Oracles/OracleOverview)).

entities.risk_posture: Pendle's own core contracts have never been drained, and PendleMarketV3 is immutable apart from pausing, which is a real strength. The risk lives everywhere else. Governance is concentrated in a 2 of 4 multisig and a single guardian key with no timelock, which was useful in September 2024 when Pendle paused everything within a day of the Penpie exploit and protected around 105 million USD, but the same power could be turned the other way. The bigger systemic issue is that PTs became collateral across Spark, Morpho, Aave and others, priced by a discount oracle that Chaos Labs showed can drift far enough for borrowers to walk away with debt, on markets running liquidation LTVs above 91%. Add underlying concentration in sUSDe and USD0++, issuers who can change redemption terms overnight, liquidity that exists only on Pendle's own AMM, and TVL that has fallen to under 1 billion USD from a 6.5 billion USD peak, and the profile is a technically sound protocol carrying other people's risks. Treat Pendle exposure as exposure to the specific underlying and to the lending market accepting the PT, not to Pendle in the abstract.

YT holders could over-collect up to `maxscale`, PT holders would receive less value in WETH terms, and LP holders would see PT prices distort. Sense airdropped roughly 11 ETH to affected PT, YT and LP holders and redeployed the adapter as Adapter 8
The Series matures June 1, 2027, well after the protocol sunset and the December 1, 2023 withdrawal deadline, and after Sense stopped hosting the interface
Every Series listed in the deployed contracts table with a 2022 or 2023 maturity has passed its maturity date; redemption depends on the Series having been settled
Both were Compound v2 cTokens accessed through the CFactory; the Sense adapters for them are deprecated with the protocol
Users entitled to MORPHO rewards could claim only up to Age 7, October 4, 2023, on a dedicated interface, and only once Morpho Governance made the token transferable

incidents.what_happened: Sense Finance announced it would sunset the Sense Protocol after 18 months of operation and open source the UI, stating that the DeFi market landscape lacked the consistent demand for fixed rates essential for robust market development. The core team ceased contributions.
incidents.outcome: Users were instructed to withdraw via app.sense.finance by 1 December 2023, after which Sense relinquished hosting of the interface. MORPHO rewards were claimable up to Age 7, ending 4 October 2023.

entities.risk_posture: Sense is a discontinued protocol, and that is the dominant fact about its risk profile. It never suffered a documented exploit, it was audited eight times by credible firms including Spearbit and Sherlock, and it was noncustodial throughout, so the technical foundation was sound. What killed it was demand: the team concluded in October 2023 that DeFi simply did not want fixed rates consistently enough to sustain the product, wound it down, and open sourced the interface. Anyone still holding a Sense position is now dealing with unmaintained contracts, a hosted frontend that was switched off on 1 December 2023, and a 2 of 3 multisig that retains real powers including pausing the Divider and backfilling the Scale value that determines how much Target each PT and YT holder receives. Layered on top are the dependencies Sense always had, on Balancer V2 for the Space AMM and on Compound or Aave for converting Target back to Underlying. The residual risk is not that Sense will be hacked, it is that no one is left to respond if something goes wrong.

entities.name: Spectra
entities.asset_strategy: Spectra is the permissionless end of the yield tokenization spectrum. Any ERC-4626 interest-bearing token can be wrapped into a PT and YT pair with no listing gate, and the protocol runs on nine networks: Ethereum mainnet, Base, Arbitrum, Optimism, BNB Chain, Avalanche, HyperEVM, Katana and Sonic, per the pool API endpoints that returned data at `https://app.spectra.finance/api/v1/{network}/pools`. Liquidity sits in Curve StableSwap-NG and twocrypto-NG pools, with a `RateAdjustmentOracle` feeding the expected PT price into the AMM so the bonding curve only has to price the deviation of the realized implied rate from the expected rate ([Spectra rate adjusted StableSwap docs](https://dev.spectra.finance/technical-reference/spectras-automated-market-makers/rate-adjusted-stableswap-pools)). The trade-off versus Pendle is stark on scale: the entire Spectra pool set returned 25 pools, and the largest, PT-yvvbUSDC on Katana, holds $380,545.80 TVL, roughly 1/130th of Pendle's largest market. The asset mix skews toward long-tail and new-chain assets (Katana vault bridge USDC and USDT, Jarvis synthetic euro, YieldNest RWA baskets, Avant avUSD on Avalanche) rather than blue chip LSDs. Spectra also formalizes negative-yield handling through a `ptRate` variable that writes down the PT's par value if the underlying IBT ever registers negative interest ([Spectra rate adjusted StableSwap docs](https://dev.spectra.finance/technical-reference/spectras-automated-market-makers/rate-adjusted-stableswap-pools)).

risks.risk: Peripheral router contract compromise
risks.description: On 23 July 2024 an attacker exploited a command in Spectra's routing utility contract that let users enter and exit pools with a token of their choice, sweeping funds once a user approved a transaction. The core protocol contracts were unaffected.
risks.current_mitigation: Router contracts were terminated, the app was disabled and Principal Token contracts paused, an incident response plan is in place
risks.monitoring_signal: Unusual approvals to Spectra router addresses, any new router deployment without audit
risks.linked_assets: ETH held in user wallets that approved the router, Principal Tokens
link_assets_unmatched: ETH held in user wallets that approved the router

risks.risk: Social engineering directing users into malicious approvals
risks.description: The July 2024 attack was amplified by a Discord user making false claims about problems with Spectra's YT contracts, prompting users to withdraw and therefore approve the malicious transaction. The attack surface was human as much as technical.
risks.current_mitigation: Incident response plan, direct communication channels, coordination with exchanges and security teams
risks.monitoring_signal: Impersonation or panic messaging in official community channels, spikes in approval transactions after such messaging
risks.linked_counterparties: Spectra Discord community, third party security teams

risks.risk: Pause authority over Principal Token contracts
risks.description: During the July 2024 incident Spectra paused Principal Token contracts to prevent token exchanges at the Curve pool level, then unpaused them roughly six hours later. That confirms a privileged party can halt PT transfers at will.
risks.current_mitigation: Pause was used defensively and reversed the same day, response documented publicly
risks.monitoring_signal: Pause events on PT contracts, duration of any pause

risks.risk: Permissionless pool creation with no vetting
risks.description: Anyone can open a Spectra pool with any ERC-4626 interest bearing token, specifying only a maturity date and target APR, with no voting or human gated process. There is no screening of the yield source behind a listed market.
risks.current_mitigation: Documented as an explicit design choice, risk documentation instructs users to do their own research on interest bearing token issuers
risks.monitoring_signal: Rate of new pool creation, share of TVL in pools whose underlying has no audit or track record
risks.linked_assets: All Spectra pools and their ERC-4626 underlyings
risks.linked_counterparties: Arbitrary third party ERC-4626 vault issuers
link_partners_unmatched: Arbitrary third party ERC-4626 vault issuers

risks.risk: Counterparty risk on interest bearing token issuers
risks.description: Spectra's own risk documentation states the protocol has no control over the tokens users contribute and instructs users to research the issuers of interest bearing tokens. Spectra is a wrapper, so the credit and peg risk of the underlying passes straight through to PT holders.
risks.current_mitigation: Explicit disclosure in risk documentation, ERC-4626 standard interface requirement
risks.monitoring_signal: Solvency and peg of each underlying, collateralisation ratio of any stablecoin underlying
risks.linked_assets: wstUSR, scUSD, stS, stXRP, sFLR and other listed ERC-4626 assets
risks.linked_counterparties: Resolv, Rings Protocol, Beets, Firelight, Sceptre

risks.risk: Concentration in a single yield source
risks.description: Spectra has historically carried heavy exposure to Resolv wstUSR markets, and Resolv was exploited on 22 March 2026 when a compromised SERVICE_ROLE key in AWS KMS allowed 80 million USR to be minted against roughly 300 thousand USDC. USR fell below 0.025 USD at its lowest point.
risks.current_mitigation: Multi chain, multi asset expansion reducing dependence on any single underlying over time
risks.monitoring_signal: Share of Spectra TVL attributable to any one underlying issuer, peg of that underlying
risks.source: [OAK Research on the Resolv USR hack](https://oakresearch.io/en/analyses/investigations/the-resolv-usr-hack-curators-face-their-responsibilities), [Spectra risk documentation](https://docs.spectra.finance/security/risk-documentation)

risks.risk: Hardcoded oracle pricing of an underlying in downstream markets
risks.description: The Resolv incident was amplified by a donation attack against Morpho vaults that priced USR and wstUSR at a hardcoded 1 USD while the real price had collapsed. Spectra PTs written against such assets inherit the same mispricing problem wherever they are used as collateral.
risks.current_mitigation: Not mitigated at the Spectra layer, mitigation sits with the downstream lending market and its curator
risks.monitoring_signal: Oracle configuration for Spectra PT collateral in external lending markets, hardcoded versus market derived prices
risks.linked_counterparties: Morpho and its vault curators, Resolv

risks.risk: Negative yield reducing Principal Token backing
risks.description: Spectra documents negative yield risk: the share value of an ERC-4626 interest bearing token can fall, which reduces the assets backing the Principal Token. A PT is not principal protected if the vault behind it loses value.
risks.current_mitigation: Disclosed in risk documentation, users can select underlyings with lower drawdown risk
risks.monitoring_signal: Share price of each ERC-4626 underlying versus its issuance value, PT redemption value versus par

risks.risk: AMM dependency for PT and YT pricing and exit
risks.description: Spectra is AMM agnostic but was launched on Curve, and PT exit before maturity requires trading against that pool. Spectra's own risk documentation lists AMM risk as a distinct category.
risks.current_mitigation: AMM agnostic architecture allowing migration to another venue, MetaVault model introducing automatic liquidity rollovers
risks.monitoring_signal: Pool depth and slippage per market, liquidity concentration around the equilibrium point
risks.linked_assets: PT and YT pools on Curve and other AMMs

risks.risk: Severe TVL contraction and fragmentation across chains
risks.description: Spectra V2 TVL stood at about 28.41 million USD spread across twelve chains, with Hemi at 13.1 million USD and Flare at 11.23 million USD together making up more than 85% of the total, while Ethereum held only about 966 thousand USD and Base about 588 thousand USD. Liquidity that thin makes any meaningful exit costly.
risks.current_mitigation: Multi chain presence capturing yield opportunities where they appear
risks.monitoring_signal: TVL per chain, share of TVL on chains with limited bridging or market maker coverage
risks.linked_assets: Hemi 13.1 million USD, Flare 11.23 million USD, Katana 1.23 million USD, Avalanche 1.15 million USD, Ethereum 966,539 USD, Base 588,110 USD
risks.linked_counterparties: Hemi, Flare, Katana, Avalanche, Base, Sonic, Hyperliquid L1, BSC, OP Mainnet, Arbitrum, Monad

risks.risk: Chain level dependency on newer networks
risks.description: The majority of Spectra TVL sits on Hemi and Flare, networks with shorter operating histories than Ethereum. A sequencer failure, reorg or bridge incident on either chain would strand the bulk of the protocol's value.
risks.current_mitigation: Deployment across twelve chains so no single failure removes the protocol
risks.monitoring_signal: Chain liveness and bridge health for Hemi and Flare, finality times
risks.linked_assets: All Spectra pools on Hemi and Flare

risks.risk: Smart contract risk in core and MetaVault contracts
risks.description: Spectra's contracts are public and audited but new components keep being added. Audit history: Code4rena on spectra-core in March and April 2024 found 0 high, 2 medium and 11 low, Pashov Audit Group in March 2024 found 0 high, 3 medium and 15 low, and Sherlock on perspectivefi metavaults-V1 in September 2025 found 0 high, 2 medium and 9 low, all fixed.
risks.current_mitigation: Three independent audit engagements with no high severity findings, all issues fixed, public source code
risks.monitoring_signal: New unaudited contract deployments, time between MetaVault feature releases and audit completion

risks.risk: Interface risk
risks.description: Spectra lists interface risk as a distinct category in its risk documentation, meaning the frontend a user interacts with may not faithfully represent the underlying protocol state. The July 2024 incident showed how interface and approval flows can be turned against users.
risks.current_mitigation: Documented as a known risk, contracts remain directly accessible
risks.monitoring_signal: Frontend integrity checks, DNS and hosting changes for the official app

incidents.what_happened: At approximately 3:00 PM UTC on Ethereum mainnet an attacker exploited a command in Spectra's router utility contract that allowed users to enter and exit pools with a token of their choice, sweeping funds after users approved the transaction. A Discord user made false claims about YT contract problems to prompt withdrawals. Four wallets were impacted and core protocol contracts were unaffected.
incidents.outcome: Spectra disabled the app, terminated the router contracts, paused Principal Token contracts to block exchanges at the Curve pool level, then unpaused at about 9 PM UTC and reinstated the app on 24 July. Authorities, exchanges and security teams were contacted, and Spectra sent the attacker an onchain offer to close the case if 90% of funds were returned. Attacker address 0x53635bf7b92b9512f6de0eb7450b26d5d1ad9a4c.

incidents.what_happened: Resolv, a major source of ERC-4626 collateral tokenised on Spectra, was exploited. A compromised SERVICE_ROLE private key held in AWS KMS combined with a completeSwap function that performed no onchain check on the ratio between deposited funds and minted tokens allowed 80 million USR to be minted from roughly 300 thousand USDC, a 266 to 1 ratio.
incidents.outcome: USR fell below 0.025 USD at its lowest point. The attacker extracted about 11,400 ETH worth roughly 24 million USD and still held about 36 million USR worth an estimated 2 million USD. Downstream damage was amplified by a donation attack on Morpho vaults using a hardcoded 1 USD oracle for USR and wstUSR. Spectra is not named among the affected protocols in the OAK Research analysis, so direct Spectra losses are n.a.

entities.risk_posture:
Spectra is a small, permissionless protocol whose core contracts have held up well and whose risk sits almost entirely at the edges. Three independent audit engagements, Code4rena, Pashov and Sherlock, produced no high severity findings, and the one exploit it suffered in July 2024 hit a peripheral router contract and four wallets rather than the protocol itself, costing around 168 ETH and being contained within six hours. The structural exposures are different in kind. Anyone can list any ERC-4626 token as a market with no vetting, and Spectra's own documentation says it has no control over what users contribute, so the protocol's real credit quality is whatever its underlyings happen to be. That became concrete on 22 March 2026 when Resolv, a major source of Spectra collateral, was exploited for 80 million USR of unbacked mint and saw USR trade below three cents. On top of that, TVL has fallen to about 28 million USD spread thinly across twelve chains, with more than 85% sitting on Hemi and Flare rather than Ethereum. Spectra should be judged one market at a time, because the protocol offers no protection at all against a bad underlying.
